title: New Skills! v1.2 brings /wait-what, /writing-for-agents, and fixes /grill-me
summary: Matt Pocock releases version 1.2.0 of his AI engineering skills repo (then the 24th most-starred repo on GitHub). The release ships a new documentation site at aihero.dev/skills, official Claude Code plugin-marketplace installation (read-only bundles with automatic updates), and openai.yaml sidecar files so every skill's user-invoked behavior (allow_implicit_invocation: false) also works in Codex. New skills: Wait What, which rewrites verbose Opus output using ASD-STE 100 simplified technical English plus grounding in the project's ubiquitous language; an updated Grill Me that asks questions in dependency-graph rounds instead of one per turn; Writing for Agents, a renamed and generalized skill for making any agent-read document concise; the Wizard skill, which generates a deterministic interactive bash wizard that walks a human through provisioning steps only a human can do; and To Questionnaire, which exports a grilling session into a markdown document non-technical stakeholders can answer.
what_you_learn: You learn practical techniques for the unglamorous side of working with coding agents: forcing verbose models into plain language, batching interview questions as a dependency graph so humans are not click-through machines, keeping agent-invoked skills out of the context window via harness sidecar files, and using deterministic scripts (not LLMs) for credential-touching setup steps.

skills.name: Documentation
skills.description: A skill for writing or improving any document an agent reads - skills, agents.md, steering files - so it is concise and the agent's output is predictable.

skills.name: Human-in-the-Loop Collaboration
skills.description: Generating a deterministic bash wizard that walks a human through steps only they can perform, like AWS provisioning and pasting API keys.

skills.name: Agent Skill Design
skills.description: Shipping openai.yaml sidecars and marketplace bundles so skills behave identically across Claude Code, Pi, and Codex.

skills.name: Domain Modeling
skills.description: Grounding agent responses in the project's ubiquitous language from glossary.md to cut verbosity and jargon.

skills.name: Token Economics
skills.description: User-invoked skills stay hidden from the agent's context window until needed, saving tokens.

learnings.title: Skills v1.2.0 launches with a full documentation site
learnings.detail: The repo (24th most starred on GitHub at the time) gets proper docs at aihero.dev/skills: the main page groups skills into flows (grill with docs, to spec, to ticket, implement, code review), a left panel gives a reference of every skill, common questions are sourced from Matt's personal wiki, and terms link into an AI coding dictionary (for example the definition of a ticket). The docs double as a way to learn AI coding concepts, not just the skills themselves.

learnings.title: Claude Code marketplace install gives read-only auto-updating bundles
learnings.detail: The skills are now an official part of the Claude Code plugin marketplace: you run plugin, search for Matt Pocock skills, and install from inside Claude Code. The result is a read-only bundle with no extra steps, and any skill updates Matt ships are automatically pulled down to users.

learnings.title: openai.yaml sidecars make user-invoked skills work on Codex
learnings.detail: Every skill now ships an openai.yaml file so it works out of the box with UIs like Codex. The key flag is allow_implicit_invocation false: user-invoked skills are hidden from the agent's context window until the user invokes them, which works on Claude Code and Pi natively but not on Codex - the sidecar makes the same behavior portable. Distinction: model-invoked skills are pulled in by the model when relevant; user-invoked ones (like the PR skill) stay invisible until asked for.

learnings.title: Wait What tames verbose Opus output with simplified technical English
learnings.detail: Matt found Opus 5 almost unreadable - incredibly verbose, full of weird LLM phrases. Fixes like output styles or agent.md tweaks did not work, so he built the Wait What skill: invoke it when the agent produces garbage and it replies with a much better alternative. The skill does two things - it instructs the agent to use ASD-STE 100 Simplified Technical English (simple language, clear declarative sentences) and to ground itself in the ubiquitous language from context.md.

learnings.title: The real cure for verbosity is your own ubiquitous language
learnings.detail: Simple-language instructions only partly work. The load-bearing part of Wait What is telling the agent to use the language the team coined in Grill with Docs - the project's own terms - instead of generic LLM jargon. Grounding responses in glossary language is what actually makes output readable.

learnings.title: Grill Me now asks questions in rounds along a dependency graph
learnings.detail: The old one-question-per-turn grilling had a horrible failure mode: at the end of a session you just say yes, that sounds good to a parade of easy questions, one per turn. The fix is multi-question rounds. The catch: question three may depend on question one. Solution: treat questions as a graph - one critical question may unlock a raft of others - and only ask the questions currently available, pushing the user as fast as possible down the frontier of the question graph.

learnings.title: Round-based grilling with recommendations makes review scannable
learnings.detail: The new Grill Me output shows round one with Q1, Q2, Q3, each with a recommended answer (with emojis for visual pop), then round two opens after round one is answered. Because Matt dictates his answers, he can blast through - Q1 agree, Q2 agree, Q3 needs a change - making the human turn nearly free while the dependency graph keeps answers valid.

learnings.title: Writing for Agents generalizes skill-writing advice to any agent-read doc
learnings.detail: The writing-great-skills skill was being used for anything an agent reads - agents.md, CLAUDE.md, other config - so it was renamed to Writing for Agents. It makes documents more concise and the agent's output more predictable, and ships with extra skill-mechanics reference material. A key use: pulling bloated front-loaded instructions out of agents.md and into focused skills.

learnings.title: The Wizard skill generates deterministic bash wizards for human-only steps
learnings.detail: Built for hated chores like AWS provisioning. The agent could theoretically do computer-use automation, but that felt icky for credentials - so the wizard generates an interactive bash script that walks the human through the exact steps only they can do. Demo: it opens the exact page needed, has you log in, paste API keys (saved to files and even GitHub secrets), and proceeds through stages with a nice UI. Crucially it is deterministic - no agent or LLM call runs in the loop, nothing is sent to Anthropic. Matt says it turned provisioning from painful to weirdly joyful.

learnings.title: To Questionnaire exports grilling decisions for non-technical stakeholders
learnings.detail: During a Wayfinder session for a garden office, Matt realized the person who needed to answer the agent's questions was his wife, not him. To Questionnaire takes the decisions a grilling session would ask and turns them into a markdown document you can paste into a Google Doc; stakeholders comment, and answers get pulled back into the agent. Matt hopes to delete the skill someday - it patches the fact that agents are hard to collaborate with (the ideal being an agent in Slack that the whole team can tag into a conversation).

learnings.title: Deterministic scripts beat agent autonomy for credential-touching steps
learnings.detail: A design principle behind Wizard: when a workflow involves secrets, purchases, or irreversible dashboard actions, generate a script with no model in the loop rather than letting an agent drive a browser. The agent plans and generates; the human executes; the script remembers state and files things in the right places.

key_points: allow_implicit_invocation false keeps user-invoked skills out of the agent's context window - and needs an openai.yaml sidecar to work on Codex.
When Opus talks garbage, do not re-read it - say wait, what.
Simple English helps, but grounding the agent in your own ubiquitous language is what cures verbosity.
Interview questions are a dependency graph - ask them in rounds, not one per turn.
End-of-session grilling dies by a thousand yes-that-sounds-good replies.
For secrets and dashboards, generate a deterministic bash wizard - no model in the loop.
Your stakeholders cannot tag an agent in Slack - so export the interview as a Google Doc questionnaire.
Pull bloated front-loaded instructions out of agents.md and into focused, well-written skills.
